stem: The chart shows union membership falling from 20.1 percent of workers in 1980 to 13.5 percent in 2000. How does the PATCO episode of 1981 fit into this longer decline?
options: (A) A landmark labor defeat — one cause within a broader decline also driven by restructuring and resistance.
(B) The PATCO firings caused union membership to rise sharply.
(C) The chart shows the PATCO episode had no effect on union membership at all.
(D) Every single American union was dissolved by an act of Congress in 1982, ending organized labor entirely.
explanation: The chart's twenty-year slide needs more than one cause, and historians supply several: the strike's defeat, plant closures, the shift toward service work, and aggressive employer campaigns. PATCO's role was catalytic and symbolic — the review's 'landmark defeat' — within a structural decline, not the sole engine of it.

stem: The review says the Reagan-era recovery brought 'stark inequality' alongside renewed growth. Which development best explains why growth and inequality rose together?
options: (A) Wages for all workers rose equally, so no inequality resulted.
(B) Tax cuts and deregulation favored investors and high earners while ordinary wage growth lagged.
(C) The federal government seized every bit of private wealth in the entire nation and forcibly redistributed it.
(D) Americans stopped working, so only investors earned income.
explanation: The Reagan program's benefits flowed disproportionately upward: lower top tax rates, deregulation's rewards to capital, and the weakening of unions all boosted returns to investors and professionals. Meanwhile, ordinary wage growth was modest — so the economy grew and the income gap widened at the same time, exactly the review's paired outcome.

stem: Which development best shows that Reagan's conservative shift outlasted his own presidency?
options: (A) The immediate repeal of every Reagan policy in 1989.
(B) A complete return to the 1970s style of liberal governance throughout the entire decade of the 1990s.
(C) A Democratic president declaring 'the era of big government is over' and signing welfare reform in 1996.
(D) The abolition of the Republican Party after Reagan left office.
explanation: Realignments are proven when the other side adapts to them. Clinton's triangulation — balanced budgets, welfare reform, deregulation-friendly policies — showed that the debate's center had moved: even Democrats now had to speak the language of limited government. That is how you know 1980 was a realignment, not a mood.

stem: The chart shows federal deficits in every year from 1980 to 1992. Reagan 'promised to shrink government at home' while 'spending massively on the military abroad.' What did this combination actually produce?
options: (A) A dramatically smaller federal government in every single respect and category, without exception.
(B) The elimination of the American military.
(C) A balanced federal budget.
(D) Redirected, not shrunk: domestic cuts, defense hikes, borrowing for the gap — per the chart.
explanation: Reagan didn't shrink government so much as reprioritize it: the axe fell on domestic social spending while the military grew, and tax cuts meant the difference was borrowed. The chart's thirteen straight years of deficit are the fiscal portrait of that redirection — smaller in some rooms, much larger in others, with debt covering the spread.

stem: On taxation, the clearest difference between Reagan's conservatism and the liberalism it displaced was which of the following?
options: (A) Liberals: progressive taxes fund programs and curb inequality. Supply-siders: tax cuts drive growth.
(B) Liberals wanted to abolish every single tax entirely while conservatives wanted to raise them all sharply.
(C) Both sides held identical views on taxation.
(D) Neither side had any position on taxes or fiscal policy.
explanation: For liberals, progressive taxes were how you paid for the New Deal/Great Society commitments and leveled the income distribution. For supply-siders, taxes were the drag on enterprise — cutting them wasn't just fiscal policy but growth policy. The same tax code was, to each side, a completely different instrument.

stem: The chart shows federal deficits rising through the 1980s, reaching $221 billion in 1986. A critic argues that Reagan's fiscal record contradicted his small-government rhetoric. Which evidence best supports the critic?
options: (A) The deficit disappeared entirely, proving the small-government rhetoric completely and utterly true.
(B) Federal debt soared while spending stayed high — government grew on borrowed money despite the domestic cuts.
(C) The chart shows that Reagan eliminated all federal spending.
(D) Deficits are unrelated to the size of government.
explanation: The critic's case is arithmetic: a president can cut domestic programs yet preside over bigger government if military spending rises and debt finances the gap. The chart's soaring deficits — debt accumulating at record peacetime rates — show a government living beyond its means, whatever happened to individual programs.

stem: The review says 'the New Right reversed the New Deal/Great Society answer to what government is for.' What did that reversal mean in practice?
options: (A) The New Right massively expanded federal social programs far beyond their Great Society levels.
(B) The New Right left the New Deal/Great Society framework completely untouched.
(C) New Deal: Washington guarantees security. New Right: limiting Washington is the goal.
(D) The New Right abolished the presidency.
explanation: The reversal was programmatic, not just rhetorical: each New Deal/Great Society instrument got a conservative mirror image — progressive taxation answered by tax cuts, regulation answered by deregulation, federal programs answered by devolution to states. The review's 'reversed the answer' is literal: the same question, the opposite policy in every domain.

stem: The chart shows the federal deficit falling from $221 billion in 1986 to $153 billion in 1989. What best explains this late-1980s improvement?
options: (A) Strong late-1980s growth lifted revenues, narrowing — but not closing — the gap.
(B) All federal taxes were abolished in 1987.
(C) Defense spending was eliminated entirely in 1988, bringing the military budget to zero.
(D) The deficit never fell; the chart is misread.
explanation: The late-1980s expansion — the long boom of Reagan's second term — swelled incomes and therefore tax receipts even at lower rates, trimming the deficit by nearly a third. But $153 billion was still roughly double the 1980 level: growth helped, yet never delivered the self-financing the theory had promised.

stem: Reagan's conservative coalition brought together which of the following groups?
options: (A) Only and exclusively Wall Street bankers, with absolutely no other supporters of any kind whatsoever.
(B) Only active-duty military officers.
(C) Only residents of California.
(D) Business, anti-communists, repudiation voters: united as much by opposition as by favor.
explanation: The review supplies all three legs: the tax-cutting, deregulating domestic program for business; the 'evil empire' rhetoric and massive military spending for anti-communists; and the 1980 'repudiation' for voters rejecting the liberal order. Each group got its priority, which is why the coalition held despite their differences.

stem: For ordinary consumers, deregulation's most visible effects in the 1980s included which of the following?
options: (A) The end of all commercial air travel.
(B) Government ownership of the telephone companies.
(C) Cheaper long-distance calls and airfares as market competition replaced government-set rates.
(D) Higher prices for every single deregulated service across the board, without any exception.
explanation: Deregulation's consumer payoff was concrete and popular: the breakup-era phone market drove long-distance rates down year after year, and airline deregulation brought discount carriers and fare wars. These visible wins helped sell the broader deregulatory program politically.

stem: The chart shows the federal deficit rising from $74 billion in 1980 to $221 billion in 1986. Which criticism of Reaganomics is best supported by the review's own account?
options: (A) That Reaganomics produced no economic growth whatsoever.
(B) Growth was supposed to pay for the cuts, yet deficits tripled by 1986 — the promise failed.
(C) That Reagan actually raised taxes sharply.
(D) That large and growing federal deficits are actually a sign of fiscal health and good management.
explanation: The fairest criticism uses the theory's own standard: supply-side economics promised self-financing growth, and the chart shows the opposite — $74 billion to $221 billion. The review's verdict holds both truths at once: growth returned, but the fiscal promise failed, which is why the deficits belong in any honest assessment.

stem: 'The new administration finally understands that business creates jobs, not bureaucrats.' — original composition in the style of a 1981 business editorial. A historian using this editorial as evidence for how business viewed Reagan should recognize which of the following?
stimulus: The new administration finally understands that business creates jobs, not bureaucrats. — Original composition in the style of a 1981 business editorial.
options: (A) It shows business enthusiasm, but as an interested source: one perspective, not the whole verdict.
(B) It proves beyond any doubt that every single American supported Reagan's entire program enthusiastically.
(C) Business editorials are never valid primary sources for historians.
(D) The editorial was written by the federal government itself.
explanation: Sourcing asks whose voice this is: a business publication celebrating a pro-business president. That makes it excellent evidence of business sentiment — the coalition's economic leg — but poor evidence for how workers, consumers, or the economy as a whole fared, which requires other sources.

stem: Reagan's domestic spending cuts targeted which of the following?
options: (A) Military spending, which was slashed to near zero.
(B) Social Security, which the new administration completely abolished during its very first year in office.
(C) Tax collection, which the administration ended.
(D) Great Society social programs, while defense grew — reversing the 1960s priorities.
explanation: The cuts had a philosophy: programs born of the Great Society — antipoverty spending, urban aid, job training, environmental and consumer regulation budgets — were the targets, while the Pentagon's budget soared. It was the New Right's reversal made fiscal: the 1960s had grown domestic government, the 1980s grew military government.

stem: Historians summarizing Reagan's domestic legacy often cite three developments together: the PATCO defeat, large deficits, and rising inequality. What connects the three?
options: (A) All three were caused entirely by foreign governments.
(B) The three had nothing in common with one another.
(C) All three expressed the rebalancing: labor→employers, revenue→debt, middle→top.
(D) All three were pure accidents of history with no relation to any policy choices whatsoever.
explanation: The three are one story told three ways. PATCO shifted workplace power toward employers; the tax-cut-plus-buildup fiscal mix shifted government's financing from revenue to borrowing; and both shifts moved income upward. Together they describe what the Reagan revolution redistributed — money and, just as importantly, leverage.

stem: Franklin Roosevelt held that government must act to secure citizens' welfare; Reagan held that government was the problem. Their core disagreement was over which question?
options: (A) Whether federal power cures economic insecurity or causes it.
(B) Whether the United States should continue to exist.
(C) Whether presidents should be allowed to give speeches to the public at all.
(D) They had no significant disagreement whatsoever.
explanation: Strip away the decades and the policies, and the two presidents answered one question oppositely. Roosevelt's answer built the New Deal state; Reagan's answer launched the project of dismantling it. Every specific fight — over taxes, regulation, welfare — was this philosophical disagreement in policy form.

stem: The chart shows union membership falling from 13.5 percent of workers in 2000 to 10.8 percent in 2020, decades after Reagan left office. What does this continuation suggest?
options: (A) That Reagan personally caused every single bit of the decline, even in the years after his own death.
(B) Structural economic forces beyond any single presidency drove the decline; PATCO was a landmark within it.
(C) That unions fully recovered their 1980 strength by the year 2020.
(D) That the chart's data must be wrong because declines cannot outlast presidencies.
explanation: The chart's post-2000 slide — under presidents of both parties — shows that PATCO lit a fire that structural forces kept burning: the economy's continued shift, global competition, and a legal environment tilted toward employers. Reagan's signal mattered enormously, but the decline's persistence proves it was never only about him.

stem: The chart shows U.S. military spending rising from $134 billion in 1980 to $299 billion in 1990. Reagan cut domestic spending while, in the review's words, 'spending massively on the military abroad.' What does the chart show about his priorities?
options: (A) He prioritized domestic social programs over defense.
(B) He cut military spending sharply.
(C) Military strength became the priority: defense doubled while small government was preached at home.
(D) The chart reveals absolutely no discernible priorities or meaningful patterns in the spending data at all, according to analysts.
explanation: The chart's more-than-doubling — $134 to $299 billion — is the fiscal proof of the review's phrase. 'Small government' described the domestic side; the military side grew to Cold War peaks. The contradiction was the point: conservatism meant a strong state for defense and a small one for welfare.

stem: The review says Reagan broke the 1981 PATCO strike 'to signal that organized labor's power was over.' What made that signal credible to private employers watching the episode?
options: (A) He praised the strikers and granted all their demands.
(B) He ignored the strike entirely and let it continue.
(C) Congress immediately overruled the president and rehired every single controller with full back pay.
(D) Skilled, irreplaceable strikers broken; traffic kept running. Even strong unions could fall.
explanation: Signals work when they're costly. Air-traffic controllers were not easily replaced — yet Reagan replaced them, decertified their union, and banned them from federal service for life. Private employers drew the obvious lesson: if the government could do that to skilled federal workers, they could take a hard line with their own unions — and through the 1980s, they did.

stem: Some historians call Reagan's 1980 victory a 'revolution' rivaling Franklin Roosevelt's in 1932. What is the strongest basis for the comparison?
options: (A) Both repudiated the old philosophy and installed a new answer to what government is for.
(B) Both winning candidates came from the same hometown.
(C) Both elections were decided by the Supreme Court.
(D) Neither of the two elections had any real lasting significance for American governance at all.
explanation: 1932 and 1980 are mirror images: Roosevelt repudiated laissez-faire and built the activist state; Reagan repudiated the activist state and began dismantling it. Both elections didn't just change parties — they changed the philosophy of government for a generation, which is what makes 'revolution' the right word for each.

stem: The chart shows federal deficits giving way to surpluses by 1998. What ended the Reagan-era pattern of large peacetime deficits?
options: (A) The abolition of all federal taxes in 1995.
(B) The elimination of the American military.
(C) The 1990 and 1993 deals (tax hikes plus restraint) plus the surging revenues of the 1990s boom.
(D) The deficits never actually ended at all; the chart is completely misread and shows absolutely no surpluses.
explanation: The chart's swing from $290 billion in deficit to $236 billion in surplus came from both sides of the ledger: the 1990 and 1993 deals raised taxes and capped spending — politically costly moves — and the tech-boom economy then flooded the Treasury with revenue. Fiscal balance returned through the very instruments — tax increases and restraint — that supply-side theory had rejected.

stem: The chart compares manufacturing's share of American jobs in 1970 and 2010. Which claim about the change is best supported by the data?
options: (A) Manufacturing's share of jobs stayed about the same across the four decades.
(B) Manufacturing's share of jobs fell by more than half between 1970 and 2010.
(C) Manufacturing output fell by more than half between 1970 and 2010.
(D) The chart proves that trade deals caused manufacturing's decline.
explanation: The chart shows 25 percent in 1970 and 10 percent in 2010. A fall from 25 to 10 is a decline of 15 percentage points, which is 60 percent of the starting level — more than half.

stem: The chart compares union membership as a share of American workers in the 1950s and the 2010s. Which claim is best supported by the data?
options: (A) Union membership grew steadily from the 1950s to the 2010s, expanding labor's share of the workforce.
(B) Unions disappeared entirely from the American workplace by the 2010s, leaving no organized labor behind.
(C) The chart pinpoints the exact year when union decline began and shows the pace of decline each decade.
(D) Union membership fell by roughly two-thirds between the 1950s and the 2010s, a steep long-term decline.
explanation: The chart shows about 33 percent in the 1950s and about 10 percent in the 2010s. A fall from 33 to 10 is a decline of about 23 percentage points — roughly two-thirds of the starting level.

stem: A historian writes: “This chart proves that offshoring caused the decline in manufacturing's share of employment.” Which evaluation of that claim is most accurate?
options: (A) The claim is correct because the chart covers the years when offshoring began and the decline is visible there.
(B) The claim is correct because offshoring is the only cause the review names for the manufacturing decline.
(C) The claim overreaches: the chart documents a trend, but explaining it requires evidence beyond this chart.
(D) The claim is wrong because the chart shows manufacturing's employment share actually growing after 1970.
explanation: The chart documents how manufacturing's share of employment changed; it does not test explanations. Offshoring is one cause the review names, but establishing that it caused the decline requires evidence connecting the two, not a trend line alone.

stem: The chart shows manufacturing's share of jobs (1970, 2010) and union membership's share of workers (1950s, 2010s). Relative to its own starting level, which measure declined by the larger percentage?
options: (A) Union membership: it fell from about 33 percent to about 10 percent, roughly a 70 percent drop.
(B) Manufacturing's share: it fell from about 25 percent to about 10 percent, roughly a 70 percent drop.
(C) Both declined by the same percentage because both ended at 10 percent.
(D) Manufacturing's share, because a 25-point drop is larger than a 23-point drop.
explanation: Union membership fell from about 33 to about 10 — a drop of about 23 points, which is roughly 70 percent of its starting level. Manufacturing's share fell from about 25 to about 10 — a drop of 15 points, which is 60 percent of its starting level. So union membership declined by the larger relative percentage.

stem: The chart shows the scale of the long decline in union membership. According to the review, which political development was tied to this trend?
options: (A) The growth of a large union voting bloc inside the Republican Party.
(B) The hollowing out of the Democratic Party's union base.
(C) The passage of new federal laws protecting striking workers.
(D) The disappearance of economic issues from American politics.
explanation: The chart shows union coverage shrinking from about a third of workers to about a tenth. The review ties that shrinkage to politics: deindustrialization hollowed out the Democratic Party's union base.

stem: The chart shows the national decline in manufacturing's share of employment. According to the review, where were the human costs of this decline concentrated?
options: (A) In the Sun Belt, where defense industries attracted new plants and population kept growing.
(B) Across all regions equally, since the decline was spread evenly throughout the country.
(C) In the rural West, where farming replaced factory work as the region's economic base.
(D) In the Northeast and Midwest, where factories closed across the Rust Belt.
explanation: The chart shows the national trend, and the review locates its costs: factories closed across the Northeast and Midwest — the Rust Belt — while growth shifted to the Sun Belt.

stem: A student points to the chart and says the 1981 PATCO firing caused the entire decline in union membership. Based on the chart alone, which response is warranted?
options: (A) The chart cannot support that claim: it shows only two points, so it cannot isolate one event's effect.
(B) The chart proves the claim, because 1981 falls between the 1950s and the 2010s, inside the period shown.
(C) The chart disproves the claim, because union membership rose after 1981 instead of continuing to fall.
(D) The chart proves unions were already gone before 1981, so PATCO could not have mattered at all.
explanation: The chart plots only two points — the 1950s and the 2010s. A two-point chart can show the overall direction of a long decline, but it cannot isolate the effect of any single event in between, including the 1981 PATCO firing.

stem: A student argues that the chart shows manufacturing jobs and union membership “declined in exactly the same way.” Which correction to that argument is warranted?
options: (A) The argument is correct: both series ended at 10 percent, so they must describe identical trends.
(B) The argument conflates two distinct measures: manufacturing's job share and workers' union membership.
(C) The argument is correct because both declines clearly had the same single underlying economic cause.
(D) The argument understates the case: the chart shows that the decline of unions directly caused deindustrialization.
explanation: The chart plots two distinct measures — manufacturing's share of jobs and the share of workers in unions. They moved in the same direction, but they are not the same trend, and the chart does not show that one caused the other.

stem: The chart shows manufacturing's share of employment falling steeply, yet the review notes that American manufacturing output stayed high. Which explanation does the review give for that combination?
options: (A) The government banned factory automation after 1970, freezing productivity in place.
(B) American firms stopped competing with foreign producers and withdrew from world markets.
(C) Productivity gains let factories produce more with fewer workers.
(D) Manufacturing employment actually rose while output fell across the same years.
explanation: The review says manufacturing output stayed high thanks to productivity gains: factories produced more with fewer workers, so employment's share could fall while output held up.

stem: The chart shows union coverage shrinking. The review says globalization replaced factory jobs with service work in retail, finance, and health care. Taken together, what does the review say about the quality of the replacement jobs?
options: (A) They offered lower wages, fewer benefits, and less security than the factory jobs they replaced.
(B) They offered higher wages and stronger union protection than the factory work they replaced did.
(C) They were broadly equivalent to factory jobs in pay, benefits, and overall job security.
(D) They were all government jobs with guaranteed pensions and lifetime employment security.
explanation: The review says the factory jobs lost to globalization were replaced by service work in retail, finance, and health care — work that meant lower wages, fewer benefits, and less security.

stem: A student reads the chart and concludes that American manufacturing output fell by more than half between 1970 and 2010. Which correction is required?
options: (A) No correction is needed: the chart directly measures manufacturing output, so the student's conclusion stands.
(B) The chart shows manufacturing output actually doubled between 1970 and 2010, so the conclusion is reversed.
(C) The chart shows union membership trends over time, not anything about manufacturing at all.
(D) The chart tracks manufacturing's share of employment, not output; the review says output stayed high.
explanation: The y-axis measures manufacturing's share of employment, not output. And the review explicitly says output stayed high thanks to productivity gains — the employment share and output moved differently.

stem: Comparing the two trends in the chart, which conclusion is best supported?
options: (A) Manufacturing workers were nearly all union members, so the two plotted trends are really just one trend.
(B) Union decline directly caused the fall in manufacturing's share of jobs shown in the chart.
(C) Both trends show the same broad change: the postwar order of stable factory jobs and strong unions eroded.
(D) The chart shows the service sector's share of total employment in both of the periods plotted here.
explanation: Both series trend downward over decades — manufacturing's share of jobs and the share of workers in unions. Together they illustrate the review's larger point: the postwar industrial order of stable factory employment and strong unions eroded.

stem: The review says the stagflation of the 1970s “destroyed the Keynesian playbook.” Why did stagflation pose such a problem for Keynesian economics?
options: (A) Keynesian tools assumed inflation and unemployment traded off; stagflation had both rising together.
(B) Keynesian economics required zero inflation at all times, a condition the 1970s economy delivered.
(C) Stagflation was caused by Reagan's 1981 tax cuts, which took effect before Keynesianism was ever tried.
(D) Keynesian economists welcomed stagflation as clear proof that their economic theories worked well.
explanation: Keynesian policy tools rested on the idea that inflation and unemployment moved in opposite directions, so policymakers could accept a little more of one to get less of the other. Stagflation — both rising together — broke that trade-off, which is why the review says it destroyed the Keynesian playbook.

stem: How did the economic breakdown of the 1970s set up the politics that followed, according to the review?
options: (A) It convinced voters to reward the party in power for its handling of the crisis.
(B) It fed the resentment that powered Reagan's 1980 victory and later populist revolts.
(C) It strengthened public faith in the Keynesian playbook as the right economic framework.
(D) It persuaded Americans that government management of the economy had succeeded.
explanation: The review draws a direct line: the 1970s broke the postwar industrial bargain, and the resulting resentment powered Reagan's 1980 victory and later populist revolts.

stem: The review uses the term “Rust Belt” for the region hit hardest by factory closures. Which description matches the review?
options: (A) The Pacific Coast states, where technology firms replaced older factories.
(B) The Deep South, where textile mills had always dominated the economy.
(C) The Mountain West, where the decline of mining drove the regional story.
(D) The Northeast and Midwest, where factories closed in large numbers.
explanation: The review defines the Rust Belt as the Northeast and Midwest, the region where factories closed in large numbers.

stem: According to the review, why did the Sun Belt attract both people and plants as the Rust Belt declined?
options: (A) Its long-established union movement and high wages drew workers to the region.
(B) Federal law required all new factories to be built in that region alone.
(C) Its defense industries, lower taxes, and air-conditioned suburbs drew both.
(D) Its cold climate and expensive housing appealed strongly to manufacturers.
explanation: The review gives three draws: defense industries, lower taxes, and air-conditioned suburbs — and says they attracted both people and plants.

stem: The review says the Sun Belt — not the old industrial core — became “America's political center of gravity.” Which chain of developments best explains that shift?
options: (A) The federal capital moved to the Sun Belt, taking national political power with it.
(B) Jobs and population shifted south and west as factory closures hollowed out the Northeast and Midwest.
(C) The Sun Belt voted as a single unified bloc in every election while the other regions stopped voting entirely.
(D) The Rust Belt's population grew faster than the Sun Belt's after 1980, shifting power back.
explanation: As factories closed in the Northeast and Midwest and people and plants moved to the Sun Belt, economic and political weight moved with them — which is why the review says the Sun Belt became America's political center of gravity.

stem: Which foreign competition does the review name as undercutting American producers during the deindustrialization era?
options: (A) Japan and West Germany, in steel, autos, and electronics.
(B) Britain and France, in textiles and shipbuilding.
(C) Canada and Mexico, in lumber and mining.
(D) The Soviet Union, in consumer electronics.
explanation: The review names Japan and West Germany as the intensified foreign competition, and steel, autos, and electronics as the industries where American producers were undercut.

stem: According to the review, which combination of developments let American firms move production abroad?
options: (A) High tariffs, closed borders, and bans on foreign investment.
(B) The breakup of container shipping and the end of trade deals.
(C) Container shipping, offshoring, and trade deals like NAFTA.
(D) Federal rules requiring factories to stay in the Rust Belt.
explanation: The review lists three together — container shipping, offshoring, and trade deals like NAFTA — as the globalization forces that let firms move production abroad.

stem: The review lists NAFTA (1994) among the forces of globalization. How does NAFTA fit the longer deindustrialization story the review tells?
options: (A) It continued an existing pattern: firms moving production abroad while factory jobs gave way to services.
(B) It reversed deindustrialization by bringing large numbers of factory jobs back to the Rust Belt states.
(C) It ended all American trade with Asia and redirected commerce toward Europe instead.
(D) It was the first event that ever connected the U.S. economy to the markets of the rest of the world.
explanation: The review presents NAFTA as one of the trade deals through which globalization let firms move production abroad — a continuation of the offshoring pattern that was replacing factory jobs with service work.

stem: As factory jobs disappeared, which sectors does the review name as absorbing workers into service work?
options: (A) Mining, farming, and fishing.
(B) Retail, finance, and health care.
(C) Steel, autos, and electronics.
(D) Defense manufacturing and shipbuilding.
explanation: The review says the factory jobs lost were replaced by service work in retail, finance, and health care.

stem: How does the review characterize the service jobs that replaced factory work, compared with the factory jobs workers lost?
options: (A) The service jobs paid more and offered stronger benefits than factory work.
(B) The two kinds of jobs were broadly equivalent in pay, benefits, and security.
(C) The service jobs were more heavily unionized than the factory jobs had been.
(D) The service jobs meant lower wages, fewer benefits, and less security.
explanation: The review is explicit: the service work that replaced factory jobs meant lower wages, fewer benefits, and less security.

stem: According to the review, what did deindustrialization do to the Democratic Party's political base?
options: (A) It hollowed out the party's union base as union membership declined.
(B) It expanded the party's union base into the fast-growing Sun Belt states.
(C) It had no meaningful effect on either party's political base.
(D) It shifted the party's base from the cities out to the farms.
explanation: The review names the hollowing out of the Democratic Party's union base as one of deindustrialization's political consequences.

stem: The review notes Reagan's firing of the striking PATCO air-traffic controllers in 1981. What signal did the review say that action sent?
options: (A) That the administration would expand federal protection for striking workers.
(B) That the strike had been settled through routine negotiation.
(C) That organized labor's power would be restored to its 1950s peak.
(D) That the new administration would not protect organized labor.
explanation: The review says the PATCO firing signaled that the new administration would not protect organized labor — a landmark defeat in the union decline it describes.

stem: The review calls deindustrialization “the economic engine under the period's politics.” Which political consequences does it trace to deindustrialization?
options: (A) The end of all regional economic differences across the country and a broad, lasting decline in political conflict.
(B) Resentment behind Reagan's 1980 win and later populist revolts, with political gravity shifting to the Sun Belt.
(C) A bipartisan consensus that ended debate over trade and globalization policy for a generation.
(D) The disappearance of the Democratic and Republican parties as national organizations.
explanation: The review's closing sentence on the topic traces three things to deindustrialization: the hollowing out of the Democratic union base, the resentment behind Reagan's 1980 victory and later populist revolts, and the Sun Belt's rise as the political center of gravity.

stem: A student claims that deindustrialization means the United States stopped producing manufactured goods. Which evidence from the review best corrects that claim?
options: (A) The review says every American factory had closed its doors by the year 2010.
(B) The review says American manufacturing output fell all the way to zero in those decades.
(C) The review says output stayed high on productivity gains as manufacturing's job share fell.
(D) The review says the United States never had a manufacturing sector in the first place.
explanation: The review distinguishes output from employment: manufacturing output stayed high thanks to productivity gains, while manufacturing's share of employment fell. Deindustrialization was a change in the structure of employment, not the end of American production.

stem: The review says the 1970s “broke the postwar industrial bargain.” Drawing only on the figures the review gives, what did that bargain look like at its height?
options: (A) An economy with no factories and no unions anywhere in the country at all.
(B) An economy where the federal government guaranteed every single worker a permanent job.
(C) An economy with a quarter of jobs in manufacturing and a third of workers in unions.
(D) An economy where agriculture employed most American workers by a wide margin.
explanation: The review's figures describe the bargain at its height: manufacturing at roughly a quarter of jobs around 1970 and union membership at roughly a third of workers in the 1950s. The 1970s broke that arrangement.

stem: Which comparison best captures the Rust Belt–Sun Belt divergence the review describes?
options: (A) Both regions lost factories at the same rate and for the same underlying reasons.
(B) The Sun Belt lost its defense industries while the Rust Belt gained new factories instead.
(C) The two regions were economically identical to each other throughout the period.
(D) The Northeast and Midwest lost factories and jobs; the Sun Belt gained people and plants.
explanation: The review's divergence is geographic: factory closures concentrated in the Northeast and Midwest while people, plants, and political weight shifted to the Sun Belt.

stem: The map above — Martin Waldseemuller's 1507 world map, the first to apply the name 'America' to the New World — best supports which of the following conclusions?
stimulus: [image] https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c0/Waldseemuller_map_2.jpg
options: (A) Europeans had fully mapped the Pacific coastline of the Americas by 1507.
(B) The name 'America' honored the Spanish monarchs who financed transatlantic exploration.
(C) Europeans had come to recognize the lands across the Atlantic as a distinct continent rather than part of Asia.
(D) Waldseemuller's map was commissioned to fix the Treaty of Tordesillas boundary between Spain and Portugal.

stem: The map above shows the routes of Christopher Columbus's four voyages (1492-1503). Which of the following conclusions is best supported by the map?
stimulus: [image] https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/fe/The_Four_Voyages_of_Columbus%2C_1492%E2%80%931503.jpg
options: (A) Columbus's voyages were sponsored by the English crown to challenge Spain's Atlantic trade.
(B) Columbus's landfalls remained concentrated in the Caribbean and along the northern coast of South America.
(C) Columbus reached the Asian mainland during his third voyage.
(D) Portuguese navigators retraced Columbus's routes to found colonies in Brazil.

stem: The photograph above shows a Spanish mission in California. The mission system best illustrates which of the following Spanish colonial objectives?
stimulus: [image] https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/9a/Spanish_mission_LCCN2017656427.jpg
options: (A) Converting Native peoples to Catholicism while extending Spanish control over the frontier.
(B) Establishing self-governing towns modeled on English colonial charters.
(C) Building a plantation economy based on enslaved African labor.
(D) Training Native peoples for service in the Spanish navy.

stem: The labor system described above differed from enslaved labor in the colonies most clearly in that it
stimulus: In the 1600s, thousands of English men and women signed contracts agreeing to work for a master in Virginia or Maryland for a set number of years. In exchange, the master paid for their voyage across the Atlantic and promised food, clothing, and shelter during the term of service.
options: (A) was organized by churches to convert Native peoples to Christianity
(B) gave workers permanent ownership of the land they farmed
(C) bound workers for a limited term under a signed contract
(D) recruited workers only from the port cities of New England
explanation: The workers described are indentured servants. Their defining feature was the contract: they agreed to a fixed term of labor, usually four to seven years, in exchange for passage to America. When the term ended, they were free. Enslaved labor, by contrast, was lifelong and hereditary, with no contract and no set end date.

stem: The planters' response to the events described above most directly contributed to which of the following developments?
stimulus: In 1676, poor Virginians - Black and white, servant and free - joined Nathaniel Bacon's uprising against the colonial governor. After the rebellion was crushed, Virginia's planter elite changed how they staffed their tobacco fields.
options: (A) the end of tobacco cultivation in Virginia
(B) a lasting political alliance between planters and small farmers
(C) Parliament's decision to outlaw the transatlantic slave trade
(D) the rapid growth of enslaved African labor in the Chesapeake
explanation: Many historians argue that Bacon's Rebellion taught Virginia's planters a lesson: a mixed workforce of poor whites and Black laborers could unite against them. In the decades after 1676, planters shifted decisively toward enslaved African laborers, who could be held for life and, under developing slave codes, could never claim the rights of English subjects.

stem: Compared with the Chesapeake colonies, New England's labor system in the 1700s relied less on bound workers primarily because
options: (A) New England merchants refused to trade with England and the Atlantic world
(B) small family farms and rocky soil made large plantations impractical
(C) the Puritan church forbade all forms of contracted labor in the colonies
(D) New England had no deepwater ports where arriving ships could dock
explanation: New England's economy was built on small family farms, fishing, and trade. The rocky soil and short growing season could not support the large tobacco or rice plantations that made bound labor profitable in the Chesapeake and Lower South, so there was far less demand for indentured servants or enslaved workers.

stem: Lincoln's purpose in advancing this argument was most likely to
stimulus: "I think the authors of that notable instrument intended to include all men... They meant simply to declare the right, so that the enforcement of it might follow as fast as circumstances should permit." Source: Abraham Lincoln, speech at Alton, Illinois, October 15, 1858.
options: (A) defend the Supreme Court's decision in Dred Scott v. Sandford
(B) argue that the founders meant equality to include Black Americans
(C) demand that Congress abolish slavery immediately
(D) argue that the Declaration of Independence had no real legal importance
explanation: Speaking during the Lincoln-Douglas debates, Lincoln used the Declaration to argue that the founders had established equality as a guiding principle that included Black Americans, even though they could not enforce it at once. The argument let him oppose slavery's expansion on moral grounds while stopping short of calling for immediate abolition, the position Illinois voters would have rejected.

stem: Lincoln's position differed from Garrison's most clearly in its
stimulus: In 1831 William Lloyd Garrison began publishing The Liberator, demanding the immediate and unconditional end of slavery. Speaking in 1858, Lincoln argued that the founders had declared equality as a right whose 'enforcement... might follow as fast as circumstances should permit.'
options: (A) the belief that slavery was morally wrong and contradicted American ideals
(B) the demand that Congress prohibit slavery in all western territories
(C) a willingness to accept gradual progress instead of immediate abolition
(D) the call for enslaved people to rise in violent rebellion against slavery
explanation: Both men considered slavery wrong, but Garrison demanded immediate abolition as a moral absolute, while Lincoln argued that the founders' promise would be fulfilled gradually as circumstances permitted. That difference between immediatism and gradualism defined the split between abolitionists and the antislavery politicians of the 1850s.

stem: Lincoln's argument about the meaning of 'all men are created equal' was made most urgent by which of the following developments?
options: (A) the 1857 Supreme Court ruling that Black people could not be citizens
(B) the admission of California as a free state through the Compromise of 1850
(C) the Missouri Compromise of 1820, which drew a line for slavery
(D) the ratification of the Bill of Rights in 1791
explanation: In Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857), the Supreme Court ruled that Black people, free or enslaved, could not be American citizens and that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories. The decision directly denied that the Declaration's promise applied to Black Americans, which is exactly the claim Lincoln was answering in 1858.

stem: The treaty's promise to bar white settlement most directly reflected which of the following?
stimulus: "The United States hereby agrees... that no white person or persons shall be permitted to settle upon or occupy any portion of the same [un-ceded Indian territory]; or without the consent of the Indians... to pass through the same." Source: Treaty of Fort Laramie, Article XVI, 1868.
options: (A) the Sioux desire to adopt American farming methods
(B) a federal plan to build new railroads across Sioux hunting territory in the 1860s
(C) the Sioux decision to leave the Great Plains voluntarily
(D) the military pressure the Sioux had applied during Red Cloud's War
explanation: The 1868 treaty followed Red Cloud's War (1866-1868), in which Lakota, Cheyenne, and Arapaho forces shut down the Bozeman Trail and forced the United States to abandon its forts. The promise to keep white settlers out was a concession the government made because it had lost the fighting, not because of any change of heart.

stem: The sequence of events described above best illustrates which of the following patterns?
stimulus: In 1868 the United States promised the Sioux that no white settlers would enter the Black Hills. In 1874, after gold was found there, thousands of miners rushed in. In 1877 Congress seized the Black Hills outright.
options: (A) the steady expansion of Sioux territory through negotiation
(B) federal courts consistently protecting treaty rights
(C) treaties giving way when settlers demanded Native land
(D) Native nations initiating the renegotiation of treaties
explanation: The pattern repeated across the West: treaties recognized Native land rights until settlers or miners wanted the land, at which point the government broke or rewrote the agreement. The Black Hills sequence - promise, gold rush, seizure - is one of the clearest examples.

stem: The discovery of gold in the Black Hills in 1874 most directly led to
options: (A) a lasting peace between the Sioux and the United States
(B) a flood of white miners into Sioux treaty lands
(C) the Sioux selling the Black Hills voluntarily
(D) Congress granting the Sioux new lands in the East
explanation: Custer's 1874 expedition confirmed gold in the Black Hills, and newspaper reports set off a rush. Thousands of miners poured into territory the 1868 treaty had reserved to the Sioux, and the army made little effort to stop them.

stem: The 1934 law marked a reversal of earlier federal Indian policy most directly because it
stimulus: The Indian Reorganization Act of 1934 ended the allotment of reservation land, restored unsold lands to tribal ownership, and allowed tribes to adopt constitutions and manage their own affairs. (Paraphrased from the Act of June 18, 1934.)
options: (A) replaced forced assimilation with tribal self-government
(B) ordered the immediate return of all treaty lands
(C) required Native children to attend distant federal boarding schools
(D) divided reservations into individual family farms for allotment
explanation: From the 1880s, federal policy under the Dawes Act tried to dissolve tribes by dividing reservations into individual allotments and sending Native children to boarding schools. The 1934 act, shaped by Commissioner John Collier, reversed course: it ended allotment and encouraged tribal constitutions and self-rule.

stem: The cartoon most directly reflects which of the following about the United States in the 1880s?
stimulus: [Image: Puck magazine cartoon, 1880, titled 'Welcome to all!' An Uncle Sam figure greets arriving immigrants at the shore.] Image: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/36/Welcome_to_all%21_LCCN2002719044.jpg (Puck, 1880; public domain via Wikimedia Commons; Library of Congress print.)
options: (A) Congress had banned nearly all immigration to the United States by the 1880s
(B) nativist groups had eliminated prejudice against immigrants
(C) business leaders opposed the arrival of immigrant workers
(D) many Americans publicly welcomed immigrants despite nativist opposition
explanation: The 1880s were the peak years of the 'new immigration' from southern and eastern Europe. Cartoons like this one celebrated the American tradition of welcome, even as nativist groups such as the American Protective Association organized against Catholic and Jewish immigrants. Both the welcome and the backlash existed at the same time.

stem: The sharp decline in the foreign-born share of the population between 1920 and 1970 was most directly caused by
options: (A) the closing of Ellis Island to immigrants during World War I
(B) the Immigration Act of 1924 and related quota laws
(C) the economic depression of the 1890s
(D) the abolition of slavery in 1865
explanation: The Immigration Acts of 1921 and 1924 set strict national-origins quotas that cut immigration, especially from southern and eastern Europe and Asia, to a small fraction of earlier levels. With fewer arrivals and no major new wave until the 1965 reforms, the foreign-born share fell steadily to its low point of 4.7 percent in 1970.

stem: Nativist movements in the United States in the 1850s and the 1920s were most similar in that both
options: (A) won the presidency for their preferred candidates
(B) focused their hostility on immigrants from Latin America
(C) directed prejudice against Catholic immigrants
(D) succeeded in ending all immigration to the United States
explanation: The Know-Nothing movement of the 1850s targeted Irish and German Catholic immigrants, warning that Catholicism threatened American institutions. The revived Ku Klux Klan of the 1920s likewise made Catholics, along with Jews, Black Americans, and immigrants, central targets of its hatred. Anti-Catholic prejudice connects the two movements.

stem: After 1965, immigrants to the United States settled in large numbers in the Southwest and the Sun Belt. This pattern is best explained by
options: (A) a federal program that assigned immigrants to western states
(B) job growth in the Sun Belt and proximity to Latin America
(C) the reopening of Ellis Island as an immigration station
(D) the decline of immigration from Asia and Latin America
explanation: The Immigration Act of 1965 ended the national-origins quotas, and immigration from Latin America and Asia grew rapidly. Many newcomers settled where jobs were expanding and where communities from their home countries already existed: the Sun Belt's booming economy and the Southwest's closeness to Mexico made those regions natural destinations.

stem: McKinley's intended audience for this argument was most likely
stimulus: "Under free trade the trader is the master and the producer the slave... 'Buy where you can pay the easiest.' And that spot of earth is where labor wins its highest rewards." Source: William McKinley, speech, 1892.
options: (A) American industrial workers whose wages tariffs were meant to protect
(B) British manufacturers seeking new American markets for their exported goods
(C) Southern farmers who favored free trade in cotton
(D) economists who opposed all tariffs
explanation: McKinley's closing line, that protection puts labor where it 'wins its highest rewards,' was pitched to workingmen. The argument was that tariffs shielded American factories from cheap foreign goods, keeping wages high. Republicans used this appeal to win industrial workers' votes in the 1890s.

stem: In the 1890s, opposition to high protective tariffs came most strongly from
options: (A) Northern factory owners protected from foreign competition by tariffs
(B) Republican leaders who championed protective tariffs in every campaign
(C) railroad executives whose businesses depended on industrial growth
(D) Southern and western farmers who paid more for manufactured goods
explanation: High tariffs raised the prices of manufactured goods, which hurt the farmers who bought them while doing nothing for the prices farmers received for their crops. Southern and western farmers, organized through the Democratic Party and the Populists, therefore demanded lower tariffs, while Northern manufacturers and Republicans defended protection.

stem: The high tariffs supported by McKinley most directly benefited
options: (A) American consumers, who paid lower prices for imported goods
(B) American manufacturers, who faced less foreign competition
(C) European exporters to the United States
(D) the federal government's diplomatic relations with trading partners
explanation: A protective tariff taxes imported goods, making foreign products more expensive and giving domestic producers room to charge higher prices without being undercut. American manufacturers were the intended and actual beneficiaries of McKinley's tariff policy.

stem: The economic changes described above most directly contributed to
stimulus: Between 1800 and 1860, canals, steamboats, and railroads linked American regions into a single commercial web. Northern factories turned to wage labor while Southern plantations expanded cotton production with enslaved labor.
options: (A) a decline in sectional tensions over the future of slavery
(B) sharper economic differences between North and South
(C) the end of cotton production in the Southern states
(D) equal wealth across all regions
explanation: The market revolution pulled the sections in opposite directions economically. The North moved toward factories, wage labor, and commercial farming, while the South doubled down on enslaved labor to grow cotton for world markets. As their labor systems diverged, so did their politics, deepening the sectional conflict.

stem: The Lowell system best illustrates which of the following changes?
stimulus: In the 1820s and 1830s, the textile mills of Lowell, Massachusetts, hired thousands of young women from New England farms. They lived in company boardinghouses and earned cash wages tending power looms.
options: (A) the movement of enslaved labor into Northern factories
(B) the decline of women's participation in the economy
(C) the shift from household production to wage labor
(D) the end of immigration to the United States
explanation: Before industrialization, most New England women produced cloth and goods within the household. The Lowell mills moved that work into factories and paid the young women cash wages, creating a new kind of worker: the wage-earning woman living away from home.

stem: The completion of the Erie Canal in 1825 most directly
options: (A) made New York City the nation's commercial capital
(B) ended the cultivation of cotton in the Southern states entirely
(C) caused the Panic of 1837 and the depression that followed it
(D) prevented the construction of railroads across the Appalachian Mountains
explanation: The canal linked the Great Lakes to the Hudson River and the Atlantic, slashing the cost of moving goods between the West and the East Coast. Trade funneled through New York City, which became the country's dominant commercial center.

stem: Holmes's statement defends which of the following constitutional protections?
stimulus: "The best test of truth is the power of the thought to get itself accepted in the competition of the market." Source: Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes, dissenting opinion in Abrams v. United States, 1919.
options: (A) the right to bear arms
(B) freedom of speech
(C) protection against unreasonable searches
(D) the right to a speedy trial
explanation: Holmes's 'marketplace of ideas' image is his most famous defense of free speech. He argued that the First Amendment protects even unpopular opinions, because truth emerges from open competition among ideas rather than from government censorship.

stem: Holmes's free-speech dissents of 1919 were most directly written in response to
stimulus: During World War I, the federal government prosecuted antiwar speakers under the Espionage Act of 1917 and the Sedition Act of 1918. Socialist leader Eugene Debs was sentenced to ten years in prison for a speech opposing the war.
options: (A) the Palmer Raids against suspected radicals
(B) the Scopes trial over the teaching of evolution
(C) the Ku Klux Klan's march on Washington
(D) the wartime prosecution of antiwar dissenters
explanation: Holmes dissented in 1919 cases, including Baltzer v. United States, that upheld convictions of wartime dissenters. His argument that the government should 'err on the side of freedom' was a direct response to the Wilson administration's jailing of critics who opposed American participation in World War I.

stem: Which of the following later developments most directly conflicted with Holmes's principle that those in power should 'err on the side of freedom'?
options: (A) the blacklisting of suspected communists in the Second Red Scare
(B) the Supreme Court's protection of criminal suspects' rights in the 1960s
(C) the passage of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
(D) the ratification of the 19th Amendment
explanation: During the Second Red Scare of the late 1940s and 1950s, loyalty programs, HUAC hearings, and Senator Joseph McCarthy's accusations cost thousands of Americans their jobs for their political beliefs and associations. Punishing people for their opinions is the opposite of erring on the side of freedom.

stem: Dunmore's offer is best understood as
stimulus: In November 1775, Lord Dunmore, the royal governor of Virginia, offered freedom to enslaved people held by rebels who would join British forces. (Paraphrased from Dunmore's Proclamation, 1775.)
options: (A) a British plan to abolish slavery throughout the empire after the war
(B) a response to colonial demands for emancipation
(C) a military tactic to weaken the rebellion through slavery
(D) an effort to recruit white colonists away from the rebel cause
explanation: Dunmore was losing control of Virginia and needed soldiers. By offering freedom to the enslaved laborers of rebels, he hoped to strip the rebellion of its workforce, frighten slaveholding patriots into submission, and gain Black recruits. The offer was a weapon of war aimed at the South's dependence on slavery, not a humanitarian policy.

stem: Despite the revolutionary ideals of liberty and equality, slavery expanded in the South during the 1700s primarily because
options: (A) the British government required the colonies to import enslaved people
(B) Enlightenment writers persuaded planters to adopt slavery
(C) indentured servants demanded higher wages than planters could pay
(D) profitable plantation crops depended on enslaved labor
explanation: Tobacco in the Chesapeake and rice and indigo in the Lower South were highly profitable export crops, and their profits depended on large, controllable workforces. Enslaved labor, which was lifelong and hereditary, gave planters the cheapest and most reliable workforce available. Economic interest overpowered revolutionary ideals.

stem: The amendment above did which of the following?
stimulus: "Neither slavery nor involuntary servitude, except as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted, shall exist within the United States, or any place subject to their jurisdiction." Source: 13th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, 1865.
options: (A) granted formerly enslaved men the right to vote in all elections
(B) abolished slavery but left freedpeople's rights undefined
(C) ordered the redistribution of plantation land to freedpeople
(D) guaranteed equal protection under the law
explanation: The 13th Amendment ended slavery as an institution but said nothing about what rights formerly enslaved people would hold. That silence left courts and legislatures to argue for years over whether freedpeople could vote, own property, testify, or move freely, a struggle the 14th and 15th Amendments later addressed.

stem: The legal uncertainty about the rights of formerly enslaved people was first addressed at the national level by
options: (A) the Black Codes passed by Southern states to control freedpeople
(B) the Compromise of 1877 that ended Reconstruction
(C) the Supreme Court's decision in Plessy v. Ferguson
(D) the Civil Rights Act of 1866 and the 14th Amendment
explanation: Congress passed the Civil Rights Act of 1866 to define freedpeople as citizens with rights to contracts, property, and court access, and then wrote those protections into the Constitution with the 14th Amendment's guarantees of citizenship, due process, and equal protection. These were the first national answers to the question the 13th Amendment had left open.

stem: The developments described above best illustrate
stimulus: After 1865, Southern states passed Black Codes restricting the movement and labor of freedpeople. Most freedpeople ended up working as sharecroppers, borrowing supplies at high interest and paying landlords with a share of the crop.
options: (A) the immediate achievement of full economic equality for freedpeople
(B) the success of the Freedmen's Bureau in distributing land to freedpeople
(C) Southern efforts to control Black labor through law and debt
(D) the rapid industrialization of the postwar Southern economy
explanation: Black Codes tried to bind freedpeople to plantation labor by law, and when federal pressure weakened the codes, sharecropping and the crop-lien system achieved much the same result through debt. Together they show how white Southerners rebuilt a coerced labor system after slavery's legal end.

stem: Eisenhower used this image to justify
stimulus: "You have a row of dominoes set up, you knock over the first one, and what will happen to the last one is the certainty that it will go over very quickly." Source: President Dwight D. Eisenhower, press conference, April 7, 1954.
options: (A) American intervention to stop communist takeovers in Southeast Asia
(B) the complete withdrawal of all American troops from the Korean peninsula
(C) negotiations to reduce nuclear weapons
(D) a policy of ignoring political conflicts in developing nations
explanation: Eisenhower was explaining why the United States was aiding France in Indochina: if one Southeast Asian nation fell to communism, he argued, its neighbors would follow like dominoes. The domino theory became the central justification for two decades of deepening American involvement in Vietnam.

stem: The domino theory most directly shaped which of the following American actions?
options: (A) the Marshall Plan's aid to Western Europe
(B) the signing of the SALT arms-control treaties
(C) the Cuban Missile Crisis naval quarantine
(D) the escalation of the war in Vietnam
explanation: The domino theory held that a communist victory in South Vietnam would topple neighboring states, so presidents from Eisenhower through Nixon treated Vietnam as a test of containment. That logic drove the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution and the buildup to more than half a million American troops.

stem: One major consequence of the Vietnam War for American foreign policy was
options: (A) a permanent increase in public trust in the presidency after the war
(B) new congressional limits on presidential war powers
(C) the end of all American military alliances
(D) the immediate collapse of the Soviet Union
explanation: The long, costly, and ultimately unsuccessful war in Vietnam shattered public confidence and led Congress to pass the War Powers Resolution of 1973, which requires the president to notify Congress and withdraw troops after 60 days without congressional approval. It was a direct legislative response to two decades of presidential escalation in Southeast Asia.

stem: The American war in Vietnam most closely resembled the Korean War in that both
options: (A) ended with a formal American declaration of victory
(B) were fought to support the spread of communism
(C) were undeclared wars fought to contain communism
(D) received unanimous support from the American public
explanation: Korea (1950-1953) and Vietnam (1964-1973) were both applications of the containment doctrine in Asia: the United States committed troops without a declaration of war to stop communist forces from taking over a divided country. In both cases the goal was to prevent communist expansion, not to conquer territory.

stem: In this passage, Washington was urging Black Americans to
stimulus: "In all things that are purely social we can be as separate as the fingers, yet one as the hand in all things essential to mutual progress." Source: Booker T. Washington, Atlanta Compromise speech, 1895.
options: (A) demand immediate voting rights
(B) organize a mass migration of Black families to the North
(C) reject all cooperation with white Southerners entirely
(D) accept social separation while pursuing economic gains
explanation: Washington's Atlanta Compromise counseled Black Southerners to accept segregation in social life for the time being and concentrate on economic self-improvement through work, property, and vocational training. The 'fingers' and 'hand' image promised white Southerners that Black workers would be loyal and productive partners in the region's economy.

stem: Du Bois's position differed from Washington's most clearly in Du Bois's insistence on
stimulus: "They are absolutely certain that the way for a people to gain their reasonable rights is [to]... insist continually... that voting is necessary to modern manhood, that color discrimination is barbarism." Source: W. E. B. Du Bois, 'Of Mr. Booker T. Washington and Others,' 1903.
options: (A) direct political agitation for voting rights and equality
(B) the abandonment of all educational efforts
(C) the use of violent rebellion against the federal government
(D) complete separation of the races in all areas of American life
explanation: Du Bois rejected Washington's counsel of patience. He argued that Black Americans must openly and continuously demand the vote, civic equality, and higher education, and must condemn discrimination wherever it appeared. Political agitation, not quiet accommodation, was his path to rights.

stem: Despite their well-known disagreement, Washington and Du Bois both believed that
options: (A) segregation laws would never be challenged
(B) the federal government should take no role in advancing Black Americans
(C) violence was the only path to change
(D) Black economic progress through work and education was essential
explanation: For all their differences over political strategy, both men placed hard work, property ownership, and education at the center of Black advancement. Washington built Tuskegee around vocational training, and Du Bois, while demanding political rights, also stressed education and economic organization as foundations of progress.

stem: These developments formed the legal backdrop for the Washington-Du Bois debate by
stimulus: In the 1890s, Southern states rewrote their constitutions to add poll taxes, literacy tests, and grandfather clauses. In 1896 the Supreme Court upheld segregation in Plessy v. Ferguson.
options: (A) guaranteeing federal protection for Black voters in the South
(B) ending all racial discrimination in the South
(C) making the response to disfranchisement an urgent question
(D) granting Black Southerners full and equal political rights
explanation: Washington and Du Bois argued while Southern states were systematically stripping Black men of the vote and the Supreme Court was blessing 'separate but equal.' The debate was not abstract: it was about how Black Americans should respond to a legal counterrevolution that was happening in real time.

stem: The territory labeled 'Mexican Cession (1848)' was acquired as a direct result of
stimulus: Map of United States territorial acquisitions, 1803-1853 (based on Library of Congress maps): Louisiana Purchase (1803), Florida (1819), Texas Annexation (1845), Oregon (1846), Mexican Cession (1848), Gadsden Purchase (1853).
options: (A) a purchase from Spain
(B) the Mexican-American War
(C) a treaty with Great Britain
(D) the annexation of an independent republic by Congress
explanation: The United States defeated Mexico in the war of 1846-1848, and the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo forced Mexico to cede California and the Southwest for $15 million. The acquisition was a conquest formalized by treaty, not a purchase like the Gadsden or a diplomatic settlement like Oregon.

stem: O'Sullivan's phrase was intended to
stimulus: "Our manifest destiny to overspread the continent allotted by Providence for the free development of our yearly multiplying millions." Source: John L. O'Sullivan, Democratic Review, 1845.
options: (A) justify American expansion across North America
(B) oppose the annexation of Texas by the United States
(C) defend the rights of Native nations to their lands
(D) promote American industrialization
explanation: O'Sullivan coined 'manifest destiny' to argue that Providence had assigned North America to the United States. The phrase gave expansionists a moral and religious vocabulary for annexing Texas, taking Oregon, and later seizing the Southwest.

stem: The Wilmot Proviso was historically significant primarily because it
stimulus: In 1846, Congressman David Wilmot proposed banning slavery in any territory acquired from Mexico. The proposal failed in the Senate, but it was reintroduced many times.
options: (A) ended the Mexican-American War in 1848
(B) admitted California as a free state in 1850
(C) created the doctrine of popular sovereignty for new territories
(D) forced slavery's expansion to the center of national politics
explanation: The proviso never became law, but it forced every politician to take a position on slavery in the territories. Northern support and Southern fury over the proposal showed that westward expansion had made slavery's future the unavoidable question in American politics.

stem: The method of protest Thoreau describes is best known as
stimulus: "If a thousand men were not to pay their tax bills this year, that would... be the definition of a peaceable revolution, if any such is possible." Source: Henry David Thoreau, 'Resistance to Civil Government,' 1849.
options: (A) civil disobedience
(B) armed insurrection
(C) judicial review
(D) party realignment
explanation: Thoreau argued that individuals should refuse to cooperate with an unjust government, even at the cost of going to jail, as he had done for refusing a poll tax during the Mexican War. Peaceful refusal to obey unjust laws became known as civil disobedience.

stem: Thoreau's argument for refusing to obey unjust laws most directly influenced
options: (A) the economic policies of the Reagan administration in the 1980s
(B) the isolationist movement of the 1930s
(C) the nonviolent tactics of the civil rights movement
(D) the expansion of the federal court system
explanation: Thoreau's essay on civil disobedience argued that conscience outranks law and that individuals should peacefully refuse to cooperate with injustice. A century later, civil rights leaders including Martin Luther King Jr. cited Thoreau when they chose sit-ins, boycotts, and marches that broke segregation laws without violence.

stem: The commission's argument for conservation rested on the idea that
stimulus: "The only proper basis for the protection of... all animals is an economic one... for the benefit of future generations of our citizens." Source: Massachusetts Commission on Economy and Efficiency, 1912.
options: (A) resources should be managed for long-term human benefit
(B) wildlife had no value to the economy
(C) only state governments, not the federal government, should protect animals
(D) hunting should be banned in all places and circumstances
explanation: The commission made a utilitarian case: protecting fish and game was 'wise economy' because it preserved valuable resources for future Americans. This was conservation for human use, not preservation of wilderness for its own sake.

stem: The commission's economic approach to conservation most closely matched the views of
options: (A) John Muir, who wanted wilderness preserved untouched by commercial use
(B) Andrew Carnegie, who opposed government regulation
(C) William Jennings Bryan, who focused on monetary policy and silver
(D) Gifford Pinchot, who favored scientific management of resources
explanation: Gifford Pinchot, the first chief of the U.S. Forest Service under Theodore Roosevelt, argued that natural resources should be managed scientifically for the greatest long-term public benefit. The commission's call for conservation 'for the benefit of future generations' is the same utilitarian philosophy.

stem: Which of the following would NOT support the claim that conservatism was politically marginal during this period?
stimulus: In 1964, conservative candidate Barry Goldwater lost the presidency in a landslide. For the next decade and a half, liberal Democrats passed the Great Society programs and held large congressional majorities.
options: (A) Goldwater's overwhelming defeat in 1964
(B) Ronald Reagan's election as president in 1980
(C) the continued expansion of Great Society programs
(D) Democratic dominance of Congress in the 1970s
explanation: Goldwater's crushing loss, the growth of liberal programs, and Democratic control of Congress all show conservatism on the sidelines. Reagan's 1980 victory shows the opposite: conservatism had returned to power. It marks the end of the marginal period, so it cannot support the claim that conservatism was marginal.

stem: The conservative coalition that elected Ronald Reagan in 1980 united which of the following groups?
options: (A) labor unions, civil rights organizations, and environmental activists
(B) isolationists, pacifists, and socialists
(C) supporters of expanded federal welfare programs
(D) economic conservatives, evangelicals, and anti-communists
explanation: Reagan's New Right coalition combined three strands: economic conservatives who wanted lower taxes and less regulation, evangelical Christians mobilized around social issues like abortion and school prayer, and anti-communists who favored a military buildup. Together they gave conservatism a mass base it had lacked in the 1960s.

stem: The founding of the Moral Majority is best understood as
stimulus: In 1973 the Supreme Court decided Roe v. Wade. In 1979, evangelical leaders founded the Moral Majority.
options: (A) evangelical Christians organizing politically around abortion
(B) a labor union formed to protect American factory jobs
(C) an environmental campaign against industrial pollution
(D) a bipartisan campaign to reduce the rapidly growing federal deficit
explanation: The Moral Majority, founded by Reverend Jerry Falwell in 1979, registered evangelical voters and lobbied against abortion, for school prayer, and for traditional family values. It turned evangelical churches, previously politically quiet, into a powerful force in the conservative coalition.

stem: Madison's reference to a 'seventh pillar' meant that
stimulus: "There seems to be no question that the issue there will add a seventh pillar, as the phrase now is, to the Federal Temple." Source: James Madison, letter to George Washington, 1788.
options: (A) seven amendments had been added to the Constitution by 1788
(B) the Constitution had created seven separate and equal branches of government
(C) seven states had voted to reject the Constitution entirely
(D) New Hampshire would be the seventh state to ratify the Constitution
explanation: Supporters of the Constitution celebrated each ratifying state as a 'pillar' holding up the 'Federal Temple.' When Madison wrote in early 1788, six states had ratified, and he expected New Hampshire's convention to add the seventh. (In the event, Maryland and South Carolina ratified first, making New Hampshire the ninth state and the one that put the Constitution into effect.) The 'pillar' image counted states joining the new government.

stem: The Anti-Federalists' central objection to the Constitution was that it
options: (A) abolished slavery immediately throughout the states
(B) gave too much power to the states
(C) built a strong central government with no bill of rights
(D) banned the formation of political parties in the new republic
explanation: Anti-Federalists argued that the Constitution concentrated dangerous power in a distant national government and lacked explicit protections for individual liberty. Their pressure forced Federalists to promise a bill of rights, which was ratified in 1791 as the price of the Constitution's acceptance.

stem: The Anti-Federalist concern about centralized power reappeared most directly in
options: (A) the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions of 1798-1799
(B) the Missouri Compromise of 1820 and its limits on slavery
(C) the Monroe Doctrine of 1823
(D) the annexation of Texas in 1845
explanation: When the Federalist Congress passed the Alien and Sedition Acts, Jefferson and Madison answered with the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions, arguing that states could judge federal overreach. The resolutions revived the Anti-Federalist argument that concentrated national power threatened liberty.

stem: In this preamble, Parliament stated that the purpose of the Sugar Act was to
stimulus: "Whereas it is expedient that new provisions and regulations should be established for improving the revenue of this kingdom..." Source: Preamble to the Sugar Act, passed by Parliament, 1764.
options: (A) grant the colonies independence
(B) punish only French smugglers
(C) end the transatlantic slave trade
(D) raise revenue for Great Britain
explanation: The preamble states the purpose openly: improving the revenue of the kingdom. After the expensive Seven Years' War, Parliament wanted the colonies to contribute to imperial costs, and the Sugar Act was the first major law designed to do so.

stem: The Sugar Act angered colonists more than earlier British trade laws primarily because it
options: (A) was never actually enforced by British customs officials at all
(B) was openly designed to raise revenue from the colonies
(C) applied only to trade with France
(D) freed enslaved people throughout the colonies
explanation: Earlier measures like the Navigation Acts regulated trade, which colonists accepted as part of the empire. The Sugar Act of 1764 was different: its preamble stated openly that it would raise revenue for Britain. Colonists read it as taxation imposed by a Parliament in which they had no representatives.

stem: The Sugar Act of 1764 was part of Parliament's effort to
stimulus: Britain's national debt roughly doubled during the Seven Years' War (1756-1763). After the war, Parliament sought new income from the American colonies.
options: (A) make the colonies help pay for war and empire
(B) reward the colonies for their loyalty during the war
(C) encourage colonial manufacturing
(D) reduce the size of the British navy after the war
explanation: Victory in the Seven Years' War left Britain with enormous debts and a vast new North American territory to administer and defend. Ministers like George Grenville concluded that the colonies, which had benefited from British protection, should contribute revenue. The Sugar Act was the first in a series of revenue measures built on that logic.

stem: All of the following helped produce the broad American prosperity of the early 1960s EXCEPT
options: (A) strong labor unions that supported high wages
(B) federal programs that expanded homeownership
(C) the stock market crash of 1929
(D) regulations that stabilized the banking system
explanation: Postwar prosperity rested on New Deal-era foundations: unions that kept wages high, the GI Bill and federal housing programs that built the suburbs, and banking reforms that prevented the panics of the past.
